changes.before: \abstract{Streaming large language model (LLM) services can expose response-length metadata even when payloads are encrypted. We evaluate a fixed T5 implementation with its recorded candidate-selection rule through 6600 reconstructions from validated application-layer length traces. For 300 aligned prompts per model, five archived-reference cohorts yield mean term-frequency cosine scores ($\phi$) of 0.482--0.535; two additional archived cohorts have malformed word boundaries. Newly generated TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini responses with verified detokenization yield means of 0.435 and 0.504. Legacy rendering of their saved token IDs reproduces all 600 corresponding archived references and length vectors. Changing both the trace and scoring reference increases mean $\phi$ by 0.356 and 0.383 under matched reconstruction settings. In two-model pilots, three of six partial-ablation contrasts remain significant after Holm correction; neither cross-prompt contrast is conclusive. Five framing transformations reduce frozen-reconstructor mean scores by 36.7--88.7\%. A five-seed study with a local empirical maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) length inverse recovers much of the loss under bucketing and batching. Reconstruction scopes and retained encoder coverage differ across these experiments. The findings quantify lexical behavior of an instrumented pipeline and demonstrate the importance of validating both observations and reference rendering. They do not measure semantic disclosure or demonstrate passive extraction from encrypted transport.}
changes.after: \abstract{Streaming large language model (LLM) services can expose response-length metadata even when payloads are encrypted. We evaluate a fixed T5 reconstructor through 6600 reconstructions from validated application-layer length traces, selecting candidates by sampling-processed transition scores through the first end-of-sequence (EOS) token. For 300 aligned prompts per model, five archived-reference cohorts yield mean term-frequency cosine scores ($\phi$) of 0.509--0.577; two additional archived cohorts have malformed word boundaries. Separately collected TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini responses with verified detokenization yield means of 0.468 and 0.527. Legacy rendering of their saved token IDs reproduces all 600 corresponding archived references and length vectors. Changing both the trace and scoring reference increases mean $\phi$ by 0.384 and 0.397 under matched reconstruction settings. In two-model pilots, four of six partial-ablation contrasts remain significant after Holm correction; neither cross-prompt contrast is conclusive. Five framing transformations reduce frozen-reconstructor mean scores by 43.8--89.6\%. A five-seed study with a local empirical maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) length inverse recovers much of the loss under bucketing and batching. Reconstruction scopes and retained encoder coverage differ across these experiments. The findings quantify lexical behavior of an instrumented pipeline and demonstrate the importance of validating both observations and reference rendering. They do not measure semantic disclosure or demonstrate passive extraction from encrypted transport.}

changes.before: The archived collector used \texttt{requests.iter\_lines()}, discarded empty lines, and appended two newline bytes to each remaining line. Its inferred vector $X^{\mathrm{col}}$ can differ from the logged vector $X^{\mathrm{log}}$: a fragment \texttt{:\textbackslash n\textbackslash n} contains three bytes, but this parser infers one. Replaying that implementation on the retained logs changes 2073 of 2100 vectors and the heuristic-segment count in 764 samples. These are preprocessing comparisons; the exact historical T5 input vectors and their binding to the old collector version were not retained.
changes.after: Every reconstruction input is an explicit vector of UTF-8 payload lengths obtained from the retained generation log. Validation recomputes each fragment's byte length, checks its ordered position and verifies that the concatenated fragments equal the scoring reference. Source hashes and immutable sample inventories bind the vectors, references and recorded seeds to the completed campaign. The experiments do not infer lengths from line parsing or undocumented historical reconstruction inputs.

changes.before: The primary results below instead come from complete T5 inference on the 2100 validated logged vectors. This establishes the inputs used for the reported reconstructions without recovering undocumented historical inputs. Differences from older scores cannot be attributed solely to collection: the execution environment and reconstruction random-state handling also differ. The reconstructor is seeded after checkpoint loading so that cache initialization does not change a sample's random stream.
changes.after: The primary cohort reconstructs all 2100 validated archived vectors with the EOS-bounded selector defined below. The two verified-reference cohorts and all control, defense and MAP conditions use the same pinned reconstruction implementation. The reconstructor is seeded after checkpoint loading so that cache initialization does not change a sample's random stream. The current campaign reuses frozen victim responses and length vectors; it does not regenerate victim responses.

These new cohorts are reported separately. Current checkpoint revisions, precision and placement are pinned; their identity with the historical execution is not established.
changes.after: To evaluate the affected models with ordinary reference text, a separate collection produced 300 responses per model from the same prompts using contextual detokenization. changes.before: The inversion pipeline follows the sequence-to-text procedure introduced by Weiss \emph{et al.}~\cite{weiss2024prompt}. It first splits a length vector at observations equal to one and merges short chunks using a ten-unit minimum, with an additional list-boundary heuristic. These are heuristic segments rather than verified sentences. The first segment is decoded using \texttt{royweiss1/T5\_FirstSentences}; later segments use \texttt{royweiss1/T5\_MiddleSentences}, conditioned on the immediately preceding selected segment. T5 generation uses stochastic sampling with top-$k=50$, temperature 1 and a two-token no-repeat n-gram constraint. The executed selector sums normalized transition scores over all returned generation steps, including PAD positions after a candidate's first end-of-sequence (EOS) token; the chosen text supplies the next segment's context.

These scores are obtained after the sampling constraints, including top-$k$ and the no-repeat rule; their sum is not an unconstrained model likelihood. The implementation does not mask post-EOS steps, which can assign nonfinite scores to a completed candidate and alter selection. A bounded replay reproduced all 24 selected first-segment predictions, but ranking only through the first EOS changed the selected text in 18 cases (Appendix~\ref{app:selector}). All three-candidate results in this paper retain the original PAD-inclusive selector. They describe this specific implementation and do not estimate the performance of an EOS-masked selector. The one-candidate MAP experiment bypasses candidate ranking.
changes.after: These scores use the sampling-processed distributions, not the unconstrained model logits. Nonfinite scores before or at EOS cause validation failure; padding after EOS does not contribute to selection. Every generated candidate is retained for independent verification; calls with three candidates also retain their transition scores. All three-candidate conditions use this rule throughout the complete response, including subsequent context updates. The one-candidate MAP experiment bypasses candidate ranking. Appendix~\ref{app:selector} reports full-campaign validation.

changes.before: Table~\ref{tab:trace_controls} shows that the effect of removing trace features depends on both model and control. For Qwen, the true-trace mean is 0.2904 versus 0.2084 after shuffling and 0.1169 for a constant trace; both contrasts are significant after Holm correction ($p=0.0053$ and $p<0.0001$). For Llama, the true mean is 0.2221 versus 0.1272 for a constant trace ($p=0.0010$). Its shuffled mean is lower (0.1798), but the adjusted signed-rank test is inconclusive ($p=0.2634$). Cross-prompt means are 0.2522 for Qwen and 0.2250 for Llama; neither contrast is significant ($p=0.3625$ and $p=0.8531$). Thus these pilots do not establish a general advantage over unrelated prompt traces. Each control retains some response-dependent information, and transformations can also alter segmentation and encoder coverage.
changes.after: Table~\ref{tab:trace_controls} shows lower scores after shuffling or constant replacement for both models. For Qwen, the true-trace mean is 0.3235 versus 0.1840 after shuffling and 0.1169 for a constant trace; both contrasts are significant after Holm correction ($p<0.0001$). For Llama, the true mean is 0.2917 versus 0.1870 after shuffling ($p=0.0002$) and 0.1252 for a constant trace ($p<0.0001$). Cross-prompt means are 0.2745 for Qwen and 0.2320 for Llama; neither adjusted signed-rank test is conclusive ($p=0.1169$ for each). The nominal mean-difference bootstrap intervals for those two contrasts exclude zero, but do not incorporate the Holm adjustment and concern a different estimand from the signed-rank test. Thus four of six contrasts support sensitivity to the altered features; the pilots do not establish a general advantage over unrelated prompt traces. Each control retains some response-dependent information, and transformations can also alter segmentation and encoder coverage.

\section{Bounded Candidate-Selection Audit}\label{app:selector}
The completed three-candidate campaign did not retain every sampled output ID and transition score. We therefore replayed 24 first-segment inputs with the original first-segment checkpoint, Transformers 4.46.3, float32 CUDA execution and saved per-record seeds. Before inference, selection was fixed to input-length extrema for two inputs from each of the seven archived and two verified-reference cohorts, plus six defense-pilot inputs covering baseline, bucketing, fixed padding, both batching sizes and random padding. This deliberately selected diagnostic set is not a random sample of the campaign.

All 24 original selected texts were reproduced exactly. The audit retained all 72 candidate sequences and step scores, and compared the executed full-step sum with a sum through the first generated EOS, including that EOS and excluding subsequent PAD. For a sequence without EOS, all generated steps are retained. The two rules selected different text in 18 of 24 cases: 11 of 14 archived inputs, three of four verified-reference inputs and four of six defense-pilot inputs. Post-EOS tails occurred in 38 of 72 candidates; each such tail included a nonfinite score, while no nonfinite score occurred before or at EOS. The normalization uses the sampling-processed scores, not the unconstrained model logits.

These findings establish that the defect can affect actual generated candidates. They do not estimate its prevalence over the campaign, a corrected full-response mean or the direction of change in any table. The original selector remains the definition of the three-candidate results reported here. Revising that definition requires replay of later segments because their context depends on the selected text. The one-candidate MAP study does not use this ranking. The supplementary \path{review_revision_20261101/ranking_audit/} directory contains the fixed input selection, complete candidate records, EOS-masking tests, protocol and audit report.
changes.after:
\section{Full-Campaign Candidate and Metric Validation}\label{app:selector}
The completed campaign retains 6600 reconstruction records, 86,788 decoder calls and 253,764 generated candidates. Of the decoder calls, 83,488 sample three candidates and 3300 produce the single candidate used in MAP. Every call records encoder inputs, generated token IDs, decoded text, the first-EOS boundary and selected text. The three-candidate calls additionally record transition scores; single-candidate MAP calls omit score computation and ranking. The audit recomputes sums through the first EOS, checks duplicate-text handling and tie order, and verifies the selected context used by subsequent segments.

Across the candidate records, 4,540,261 generated positions contribute to the selector scores. A total of 142,629 candidates have a returned tail after their first EOS, comprising 393,353 excluded positions. Each such tail includes a nonfinite processed score; no nonfinite score enters an EOS-bounded sum. Candidates without EOS retain all returned generation steps. These counts describe the complete retained candidate inventory. They do not measure semantic correctness or compare alternative ranking objectives.

Independent checks reproduce the reconstruction metrics, cohort summaries and statistical intervals from the current predictions. All requested archived and verified-reference segments were attempted; the archived cohort contains two empty terminal selections, which are retained in its scored outputs. The audit also verifies all 3900 secondary records and their source bindings. The accompanying supplementary verifier provides checks of these current outputs without GPU inference; full reproduction additionally requires the pinned model weights and recorded execution environment.

changes.before: The control and defense experiments use explicit BLAKE2s-derived, condition-specific decoder seeds and record every seed and transformed vector. Shuffling uses seed $20260706+17i$ for prompt index $i$. Cross-prompt inputs cycle the trace of donor index $(i\bmod30)+1$ to the target's trace length. Random padding has a separately recorded transformation seed, and its payload overhead is calculated from the actual saved padding realization. These are newly specified pilot random draws, not recovered historical seeds. The control and defense baseline reconstructions use distinct decoder seeds, so even their identical undefended length traces can yield different mean scores. Historical \texttt{hash()}-dependent seeds and inconsistent padding-cost summaries are excluded from the current results.
